Retention, deletion, and storage reclamation

This page describes v0.4.2, the latest supported release. v0.3.3 is withdrawn and unsupported; its public artifacts remain available for forensic or compatibility inspection and must not be deployed. v0.4.2 retains v0.4.0's retraction of v0.3.3. v0.3.2 has DLQ retention and automatic local reclamation, but the work budgets below describe v0.4.2 unless a version difference is stated. v0.3.2 does not have the queue and subscription lifecycle APIs introduced in v0.4.0.

What removes retained messages

Default Peek-Lock delivery is at-least-once. Receive-and-delete is the explicit at-most-once broker-removal alternative and removes a message before returning it; retrying the same receive attempt ID can replay its saved response. A durable message stays retained until a documented lifecycle action removes or moves it:

Stored state Normal lifecycle Other authorized removal
active Receive, then Complete or receive-and-delete message TTL with discard; forced queue/subscription deletion; subscription expiry
locked Complete, or lock expiry returns it to active / moves it to the DLQ at the delivery limit message TTL with discard; forced queue/subscription deletion; subscription expiry
deferred ReceiveDeferred, then settle message TTL with discard; forced queue/subscription deletion; subscription expiry
scheduled activation at its due time; Cancel only for a scheduled send that has never been delivered message TTL with discard; forced queue/subscription deletion; subscription expiry
dead_lettered Redrive or Purge configured DLQ retention; forced queue/subscription deletion; subscription expiry

Complete and receive-and-delete remove the row immediately. A message TTL either moves an expired message to the DLQ or discards it according to dead_letter_on_expire. The queue default is also a ceiling for an explicit Send TTL. Its clock starts at the message's initial visibility time, so scheduled waiting does not consume it; later delayed Abandon does not restart it. Expired locks are reclaimed by the reaper and can be delivered again, so consumers must be idempotent.

Deduplication rows, settlement receipts, and receive-attempt records have their own expiry-based background cleanup. They are operational replay metadata, not a message archive; those expiry deletes are not row-budgeted per pass.

DLQ retention

mqlite serve applies default retention targets to dead letters. Every 60 seconds the retention worker deletes the oldest matching dead letters in bounded batches. These are asynchronous cleanup targets, not admission limits: a queue can temporarily exceed its age, count, or byte target between passes or while cleanup catches up. The worker never deletes active, locked, deferred, or scheduled rows.

Setting Broker default Meaning
MQLITE_DLQ_MAX_AGE 336h (14 days) delete dead letters older than this, measured from original enqueue time
MQLITE_DLQ_MAX_COUNT 1000000 per queue keep at most this many dead letters
MQLITE_DLQ_MAX_BYTES 0 optional per-queue cap on dead-letter body bytes; zero disables this bound
MQLITE_DLQ_RETENTION enabled set to off to disable all broker defaults

Embedded engines leave engine-wide DLQ retention defaults disabled unless the application passes WithDLQRetention(maxAge, maxCount, maxBytes). A positive per-queue bound still enables that dimension for its queue.

Each queue can override the engine or broker defaults through QueueConfig, the wire config object, or mqlite create-queue:

Per-queue value Effective behavior
0 inherit the engine or broker default
positive use this queue-specific bound
negative explicitly leave that dimension unbounded

The fields are dlq_max_age_ms, dlq_max_count, and dlq_max_bytes. Age uses enqueued_at, not the time at which the message entered the DLQ. Count and byte limits drop the oldest dead letters first.

Monitor DLQ count, age, and storage size even when defaults are enabled. A growing active backlog is a consumer-capacity problem and is deliberately outside the DLQ retention policy.

Queue and subscription retirement

On main, queue and subscription deletion is empty-only by default. force=true is durable authorization to discard all retained states, including locked work, plus resource-owned deduplication and replay metadata. A locked delivery may already have caused an external effect; deleting its row cannot undo that effect.

A fixed subscription TTL grants the same discard authorization in advance. Its absolute deadline is saved on first creation and does not move when the filter is updated, a message is published or received, or creation is retried. At the deadline the subscription immediately leaves topic fan-out and its data plane. Physical cleanup follows in the background. Explicit deletion remains the normal completion path; TTL is a forgotten-cleanup backstop.

The accepting transaction changes the resource to deleting and starts bounded cleanup. If that cleanup finishes, the same commit removes the resource and the call returns deleted; otherwise the committed deleting marker reserves the name while restart-safe cleanup removes its rows. The foreground request removes at most 1,000 rows and targets about 8 MiB. Each continuation pass removes at most 4,096 physical rows and targets about 8 MiB. Its ordinary per-resource path visits at most 32 local resources, or one such resource on remote Turso/libSQL. A separate set-based path can finalize up to 512 empty subscriptions without consuming that 32-or-1 resource-count allowance; their mapping and backing queue rows still consume the shared row budget. One oversized row may exceed the byte target so cleanup can still make progress.

The default subscription capacity is 10,000 active plus deleting mappings. A mapping continues to occupy a slot until physical cleanup finishes. Large forced deletes or simultaneous expiry waves can therefore create cleanup backlog, grow the WAL, delay name reuse, and temporarily reject new subscription creation.

For routine request/reply traffic, keep a stable reply subscription and dispatch with correlation_id. If a temporary subscription is necessary, use a globally unique one-use name, delete it explicitly when finished, add a fixed TTL as a backstop, and stagger deadlines. Drain before deletion when practical. Reserve force for intentional abandonment.

One controller must serialize deletion and same-name recreation. After an uncertain response, use the read-only paged inventory with deleting entries included. Wait until the name is absent before recreating it, and do not replay an old delete after a replacement exists.

Local file reclamation

Deleting a row makes SQLite pages reusable immediately; it does not promise that the database or WAL file will shrink at once. New local databases use auto_vacuum=INCREMENTAL.

On main, the background reclaimer runs every 60 seconds. Once at least 256 pages are free, it checkpoints and returns at most 256 pages per pass to the operating system. One-off large deletions can therefore need several passes. v0.3.2 uses the same interval and threshold but attempts to drain the current freelist in one pass; it does not have main's 256-page work cap. WAL size can also grow while a reader holds a snapshot, then shrink after checkpointing when that reader finishes.

Operator commands provide explicit reclamation:

  • mqlite vacuum checkpoints and exhausts the current incremental-vacuum freelist. It is the normal manual choice after a large purge.
  • mqlite vacuum --full rewrites the database and holds the global writer. Use it only in a deliberate maintenance window.

Remote Turso/libSQL manages its physical storage. The client does not expose its database or WAL file size, and local vacuum commands do not apply.

Size local storage for the peak simultaneous backlog, WAL growth, backup space, and the time needed for bounded cleanup and reclamation. Alert on free disk, retained/deleting inventory, maintenance failures, and oldest message age rather than assuming file size will fall immediately after a delete.

Exporting dead letters before deletion

MQLite has no built-in archive sink. An operator can use existing operations:

  1. Quiesce or otherwise coordinate changes to the selected DLQ range.
  2. Read dead letters with Peek(state=dead_lettered), advancing from past the last exported sequence number, and durably write them to external storage.
  3. Verify the external copy.
  4. After quiescing, purge only after the export covers the intended DLQ. Use max or older_than bounds where appropriate. Alternatively, Redrive to a queue whose consumer writes each message to the archive before completing it.

Peek is non-destructive and does not make the export and purge one transaction. Redrive moves each selected internal batch atomically: source deletion and target insertion commit together. Delivery from the dedicated queue to an external archive remains at-least-once, so the archive consumer must be idempotent; Redrive does not make the external archival handoff one transaction.
